articles.title: Three giant black holes discovered in a galaxy from the dawn of time
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding black holes inside a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years away, revealing a remarkable scene from the universe’s infancy. Two of the black holes are separated by just 620 light-years and are expected to eventually merge, while a third lurks farther away. One weighs an astonishing 80 million suns, and another is growing faster than conventional theories predict.
articles.content:
Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding supermassive black holes in a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years from Earth. The finding, made by an international research team led by the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics (MPE), offers a rare glimpse of how enormous black holes grew and interacted during the universe's earliest stages.

The black holes are located in a galaxy known as J0148-4214. All three are actively accumulating matter, which spirals toward them through surrounding disks of gas and other material. Because the galaxy is so distant, its light has traveled through space for approximately 12.5 billion years before reaching Earth. This means astronomers are observing it as it existed just 1.2 billion years after the Big Bang.

Over such vast distances, the expansion of the universe stretches light to longer, redder wavelengths. Astronomers measure this effect through a property called redshift. For J0148-4214, the researchers measured a redshift of z=5.02, allowing them to determine its remarkable distance.

Three Black Holes in One Ancient Galaxy

"This is the first evidence of three active black holes in a single galaxy in the distant Universe," says Hannah Übler, research group leader at MPE and lead author of the study.

Two of the black holes lie near the galaxy's center, separated by a projected distance of just 620 light-years. The third is much farther out, approximately 5,500 light-years from the center.

The discovery provides important evidence about how massive black holes came together in the young universe.

"It suggests that processes in the early Universe were efficient at bringing massive black holes together, setting the stage for the massive black hole mergers we expect to detect with future gravitational wave observatories," says Übler.

Astronomers believe that galaxy collisions and mergers were common during the universe's early history. As galaxies combined, their central black holes could also move closer together and eventually merge. These mergers would produce increasingly massive black holes at the centers of the newly formed galaxies, potentially helping explain how some grew to enormous sizes so soon after the Big Bang.

How Astronomers Detected the Hidden Black Holes

The researchers identified the three black holes by examining distinctive patterns in the light emitted by hydrogen gas. Near a black hole, powerful gravitational forces cause gas to move at extremely high speeds. These movements leave recognizable signatures in the spectrum of light, allowing astronomers to detect black hole activity even when the objects themselves cannot be seen directly.

In the center of J0148-4214, the team found a particularly complicated hydrogen emission pattern. The best explanation was the presence of two closely spaced black holes rather than a single source.

To distinguish between them, the scientists used a precise measurement technique called spectro-astrometry. By tracking subtle changes in the positions of spectral emissions across the galaxy, they were able to identify the locations of both central black holes, even though the telescope could not resolve them as two separate points of light.

The observations also revealed the third active black hole in the galaxy's outer region.

Three Black Holes With Remarkably Different Masses

The three black holes vary dramatically in size. According to the researchers' calculations, their masses are approximately 80 million, 600,000, and 2 million times that of the Sun.

Surprisingly, the largest black hole is not the one feeding most aggressively. Its smaller neighbor, with a mass of roughly 600,000 suns, is accumulating matter at a much higher rate. In fact, its estimated feeding rate exceeds the maximum predicted by basic models of black hole growth (the Eddington limit).

This unusually rapid growth may offer clues to how some black holes became extraordinarily massive during the relatively short time available in the early universe.

"The JWST data allowed us not only to identify the three black holes, but also to estimate their masses, accretion rates, and the stellar mass of the galaxy," says Dr. Giovanni Mazzolari, second author of the study and researcher at MPE. "We find a total stellar mass of about 1.3 billion suns, and the black holes represent a significant fraction of that."

An Ancient Black Hole Merger in the Making

The two black holes near the galaxy's center are expected to merge within the next few hundred million years. Their eventual collision could help produce an even more massive black hole, illustrating a process that may have been essential to the growth of the universe's earliest cosmic giants.

"These results are extremely exciting," adds Roberto Maiolino, professor at the University of Cambridge and co-author of the study. "They suggest that black hole merging may be an additional, fast route for their rapid growth in the early Universe."

The third black hole presents another intriguing puzzle. Located well outside the galaxy's center, it could be a remnant of an earlier merger that was pushed outward by a powerful gravitational recoil. Such a kick can occur when merging black holes emit gravitational waves unevenly, sending the resulting black hole in the opposite direction.

Another possibility is that the third black hole is gradually moving toward the galaxy's center, where it may eventually interact with the other two.

James Webb Reveals Black Holes That Might Otherwise Remain Hidden

The discovery highlights the remarkable capabilities of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) for studying black holes in distant galaxies.

In particular, the findings demonstrate the importance of integral field spectroscopy, which allows astronomers to examine how light and its spectral signatures vary across different parts of a galaxy.

Using Webb's Near Infrared Spectrograph in its integral field spectroscopy mode (NIRSpec-IFS), the researchers were able to separate signals that would otherwise have appeared to come from a single black hole.

Without that detailed spatial information, astronomers likely would have identified only one of the galaxy's three active black holes.

The results suggest that other distant galaxies may contain multiple growing black holes that have gone undetected. Finding more of these hidden systems could help scientists reconstruct the history of black hole mergers and better understand how the universe produced its most massive black holes so early in cosmic history.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant astronomical discovery of three actively feeding supermassive black holes in a single distant galaxy from the early universe, providing new insights into black hole growth and galaxy evolution. This finding has broad scientific importance for understanding cosmic history and the formation of massive black holes, with detailed context and implications described.
articles.personality_title: Astronomers find three giant black holes in one ancient galaxy
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists study black holes to learn how they grow and affect galaxies. Black holes are regions in space with strong gravity that even light cannot escape. Finding multiple big black holes in one galaxy, especially from the early universe, helps us understand how the universe developed.

**What happened** – Researchers led by the Max Planck Institute discovered three supermassive black holes actively feeding on matter inside a galaxy called J0148-4214. This galaxy is over 12.5 billion light-years away, meaning we see it as it was just 1.2 billion years after the Big Bang. Two of the black holes are very close, only 620 light-years apart, and a third lies farther out. Their sizes range from 600,000 to 80 million times the mass of our Sun.

**Impact** – This is the first time three active black holes have been found in one distant galaxy. It shows that black holes could come together and grow quickly in the early universe. One smaller black hole is feeding faster than expected by current theories, which might explain how some black holes became so huge so fast. The discovery also hints that black holes merging was a key way they grew bigger.

**What's next step** – The two close black holes will likely merge in a few hundred million years, forming an even larger black hole. Scientists will continue using the James Webb Space Telescope to look for more galaxies with multiple black holes. This will help them understand how common these black hole groups are and how they shaped galaxy growth.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Three giant black holes feeding in one ancient galaxy reveal new clues about how black holes grew and merged in the early universe.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des astronomes découvrent trois énormes trous noirs dans une galaxie ancienne
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques étudient les trous noirs pour comprendre comment ils grandissent et influencent les galaxies. Un trou noir est une région de l'espace où la gravité est si forte que même la lumière ne peut s'en échapper. Trouver plusieurs gros trous noirs dans une même galaxie, surtout dans l'univers primitif, aide à comprendre l'évolution de l'univers.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Une équipe dirigée par l'Institut Max Planck a découvert trois trous noirs supermassifs qui absorbent activement de la matière dans une galaxie appelée J0148-4214. Cette galaxie est située à plus de 12,5 milliards d'années-lumière, ce qui signifie que nous la voyons telle qu'elle était il y a seulement 1,2 milliard d'années après le Big Bang. Deux trous noirs sont très proches, à seulement 620 années-lumière, et un troisième est plus éloigné. Leur masse varie de 600 000 à 80 millions de fois celle du Soleil.

**Impact** – C'est la première fois que trois trous noirs actifs sont découverts dans une galaxie aussi lointaine. Cela montre que les trous noirs pouvaient se rapprocher et grandir rapidement dans l'univers jeune. Un des plus petits trous noirs absorbe de la matière plus vite que prévu, ce qui pourrait expliquer comment certains trous noirs sont devenus très grands si vite. La découverte suggère aussi que la fusion des trous noirs était un moyen important pour leur croissance.

**Prochaine étape** – Les deux trous noirs proches devraient fusionner dans quelques centaines de millions d'années, formant un trou noir encore plus grand. Les chercheurs continueront d'utiliser le télescope spatial James Webb pour chercher d'autres galaxies avec plusieurs trous noirs. Cela aidera à savoir si ces groupes de trous noirs sont fréquents et comment ils ont influencé la croissance des galaxies.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Trois énormes trous noirs actifs dans une galaxie ancienne offrent de nouveaux indices sur la croissance et la fusion des trous noirs dans l'univers primitif.
articles.personality_title_es: Astrónomos encuentran tres enormes agujeros negros en una galaxia antigua
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos estudian los agujeros negros para entender cómo crecen y afectan a las galaxias. Un agujero negro es una zona en el espacio con gravedad tan fuerte que ni la luz puede escapar. Encontrar varios agujeros negros grandes en una sola galaxia, especialmente del universo temprano, ayuda a comprender cómo se formó el universo.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo liderado por el Instituto Max Planck descubrió tres agujeros negros supermasivos que están absorbiendo materia activamente dentro de una galaxia llamada J0148-4214. Esta galaxia está a más de 12.5 mil millones de años luz, lo que significa que la vemos como era hace solo 1.2 mil millones de años después del Big Bang. Dos de los agujeros negros están muy cerca, a solo 620 años luz, y un tercero está más lejos. Sus tamaños van desde 600,000 hasta 80 millones de veces la masa del Sol.

**Impacto** – Es la primera vez que se encuentran tres agujeros negros activos en una galaxia tan lejana. Esto muestra que los agujeros negros podían juntarse y crecer rápido en el universo joven. Un agujero negro más pequeño está absorbiendo materia más rápido de lo que las teorías actuales predicen, lo que podría explicar cómo algunos agujeros negros se hicieron tan grandes tan rápido. El hallazgo también sugiere que las fusiones de agujeros negros fueron una forma importante de crecer.

**Próximo paso** – Se espera que los dos agujeros negros cercanos se fusionen en unos cientos de millones de años, formando un agujero negro aún más grande. Los científicos seguirán usando el telescopio espacial James Webb para buscar más galaxias con varios agujeros negros. Esto ayudará a saber qué tan comunes son estos grupos y cómo influyeron en el crecimiento de las galaxias.

**Mensaje en una frase** – Tres enormes agujeros negros activos en una galaxia antigua revelan nuevas pistas sobre cómo crecieron y se fusionaron los agujeros negros en el universo temprano.

articles.title: Astronomers may have discovered the first moon beyond our Solar System
articles.summary: Astronomers have uncovered evidence of a bizarre, potentially historic discovery: the first moon ever detected beyond our Solar System. Unlike familiar moons, this mysterious object is at least as massive as Jupiter and orbits a brown dwarf, which itself circles a star. The unusual arrangement challenges traditional definitions of planets and moons, leaving scientists unsure what to call it.
articles.content:
Astronomers may have found the first moon beyond our Solar System, but the mysterious object is unlike any moon we know. Observations from the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (ESO's VLT) have uncovered evidence of an enormous moon-like body in the CD-35 2722 star system. Rather than orbiting a planet, this unusual object circles a brown dwarf, a celestial body more massive than a planet but not massive enough to become a star.

If confirmed, the discovery could mark the first detection of a natural satellite outside our Solar System, potentially changing how astronomers define moons and planets.

A Bizarre Star System Unlike Our Own

Kevin Hoy, an ESO student based in Chile and lead author of the study published in Nature, spent months examining the CD-35 2722 system. He describes its unusual arrangement as "super weird" compared with our own Solar System.

At the center of this relatively young system is CD-35 2722, a star with approximately half the Sun's mass. Orbiting the star is a brown dwarf, an object that occupies the murky boundary between planets and stars. Brown dwarfs are generally too small to sustain the hydrogen fusion that powers ordinary stars, yet they are more massive than planets.

The newly identified object orbits this brown dwarf, creating a remarkable arrangement in which a massive satellite circles an object that itself revolves around a star.

"This system is somewhat hard to define using Solar-System-based words like 'planet' and 'moon'," states Hoy, who is also affiliated with the Universidad Diego Portales and the Millennium Nucleus of Young Exoplanets and their Moons (YEMS) in Chile.

The researchers refer to the newly detected object as an exosatellite. It has at least as much mass as Jupiter, while the brown dwarf it orbits is more than 30 times as massive as Jupiter. This makes the possible moon far more massive than any natural satellite in our Solar System.

"The exosatellite is clearly massive enough to be a planet, but it does not orbit a star, though it orbits an object that orbits a star," says Hoy. "Being the third wheel in this system makes us want to call it a moon, even if it is nothing like the small, rocky moons we have in our system."

A Giant Exomoon That Challenges Cosmic Definitions

The unusual discovery highlights a fundamental problem with applying familiar astronomical labels to objects found in distant star systems.

An exosatellite is a natural satellite located beyond our Solar System, while the term exomoon generally refers to a natural satellite orbiting a planet or another celestial body outside our Solar System. However, astronomers have not established a universally accepted definition of an exomoon.

That distinction becomes especially important in the CD-35 2722 system, where the possible moon is itself massive enough to be considered a planet under some classification schemes.

Alice Zurlo, director of YEMS and a collaborator on the study, explains: "The satellite we report is a giant gaseous body orbiting a highly massive companion, itself several times the mass of Jupiter."

The arrangement is very different from the familiar structure of our Solar System, where planets orbit the Sun and moons orbit planets.

"We have a clear delineation between the planets and the Sun in the Solar System, so defining things like moons is simple. In the CD-35 2722 system, where we are blurring the lines between stars, planets, and moons, the whole thing becomes more complicated to describe," adds Zurlo, who is also an astrophysicist at Universidad Diego Portales.

Scientists Search for the First Confirmed Exomoon

Astronomers have spent years looking for moons around objects beyond our Solar System, but no candidate has yet been detected with enough certainty to establish a confirmed discovery.

That makes the latest findings particularly significant. Although scientists have identified more than 6,000 exoplanets, only a handful of possible exomoons have emerged from observations, and the evidence supporting them remains limited.

Earlier in 2026, a research team led by Quentin Kral reported possible signs of a satellite in the HD 206893 star system. Their observations, obtained with ESO's Very Large Telescope Interferometer, suggested that a moon-like companion might exist, but they did not establish a definitive detection.

The CD-35 2722 system now offers another promising opportunity, supported by measurements of how the suspected moon affects the motion of its larger companion.

How Astronomers Detected the Possible Alien Moon

To investigate CD-35 2722, Hoy, Zurlo, and their colleagues used the CRIRES+ instrument installed on ESO's Very Large Telescope.

The team applied a technique known as the radial velocity method, which was also used to discover the first exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star.

This approach works by measuring extremely small changes in an object's motion. When two celestial bodies orbit one another, their mutual gravitational attraction causes both to move around a shared center of mass. Even a much smaller companion can produce a detectable wobble in the larger object's motion.

By examining subtle changes in the brown dwarf's motion, the researchers identified what they consider strong evidence that another massive body is orbiting it.

"As exotic as it is, this system is truly unique and represents a breakthrough: the first plausible detection of an exosatellite," says Zurlo.

A New Era in the Search for Alien Moons

Confirming moons beyond our Solar System would do more than add another category of objects to astronomical catalogs. These discoveries could help researchers understand how planetary systems form, how their components interact, and why some systems develop structures dramatically different from our own.

Future observations could also reveal whether massive satellites like the one proposed in CD-35 2722 are rare exceptions or part of a much broader population of unusual celestial objects.

ESO's upcoming Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) is expected to play a major role in that search. Equipped with an enormous 39-meter mirror and advanced scientific instruments, the telescope will give astronomers the ability to detect smaller exomoons that are currently beyond the reach of existing observatories.

As scientists begin identifying more satellites in distant planetary systems, they may discover that familiar distinctions between stars, planets, and moons are not as universal as once assumed.

What Counts as an Exomoon?

A satellite is any object that travels around another object. Satellites can be natural (like our own moon) or artificial (like a spacecraft).

An exosatellite is a satellite located outside our Solar System. The term exomoon generally describes a natural satellite orbiting a planet or another object beyond our Solar System, although astronomers have not agreed on an official definition.

The possible companion in CD-35 2722 illustrates why that definition matters. With a mass comparable to or greater than Jupiter's, it resembles a planet in size and composition, yet its orbital relationship with the brown dwarf makes it a candidate for an entirely different classification.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a potentially historic scientific discovery—the first plausible detection of a moon beyond our Solar System—which could significantly advance our understanding of planetary systems and celestial classifications. The discovery has broad significance for astronomy and space science, is based on detailed observations and analysis, and represents a meaningful breakthrough with potential large-scale impact on scientific knowledge.
articles.personality_title: Astronomers find a giant possible moon outside our Solar System
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have been searching for moons beyond our Solar System for many years. While thousands of planets have been found orbiting other stars, finding moons around those planets has been much harder. 

**What happened** – Using a powerful telescope in Chile, astronomers discovered a very large object orbiting a brown dwarf, which itself orbits a star called CD-35 2722. This object is at least as big as Jupiter, making it much bigger than any moon we know. Because it orbits a brown dwarf (which is between a planet and a star), scientists are calling it an exosatellite. This is the first time such a possible moon has been detected beyond our Solar System.

**Impact** – This discovery is unusual because the object is huge and doesn’t fit neatly into the categories of planet or moon based on what we see in our Solar System. It challenges how scientists define moons and planets. Finding such an exosatellite helps us learn more about how different star systems can be organized and how they form.

**What's next step** – Astronomers will continue studying the CD-35 2722 system to confirm the object is really a moon and not something else. New telescopes, like the upcoming Extremely Large Telescope, will help find more moons around distant stars and give clearer pictures of these strange systems.

**One-sentence takeaway** – For the first time, astronomers have found strong evidence of a giant moon orbiting a brown dwarf beyond our Solar System, changing how we understand moons and planets in space.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les astronomes découvrent une possible énorme lune hors de notre Système solaire
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques cherchent depuis des années des lunes en dehors de notre Système solaire. Bien que des milliers de planètes aient été découvertes autour d’autres étoiles, il est beaucoup plus difficile de trouver des lunes autour de ces planètes.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Grâce à un puissant télescope au Chili, des astronomes ont découvert un objet très grand qui orbite autour d’une naine brune, elle-même en orbite autour d’une étoile appelée CD-35 2722. Cet objet est au moins aussi gros que Jupiter, bien plus grand que toutes les lunes que nous connaissons. Comme il orbite une naine brune (qui est entre une planète et une étoile), les scientifiques l’appellent un exosatellite. C’est la première fois qu’une telle lune possible est détectée en dehors de notre Système solaire.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est inhabituelle car l’objet est énorme et ne correspond pas clairement aux catégories de planète ou lune basées sur notre Système solaire. Cela remet en question la façon dont les scientifiques définissent les lunes et les planètes. Trouver un tel exosatellite nous aide à mieux comprendre comment les différents systèmes stellaires peuvent s’organiser et se former.

**Étape suivante** – Les astronomes continueront d’étudier le système CD-35 2722 pour confirmer que l’objet est vraiment une lune et non autre chose. De nouveaux télescopes, comme le futur Extremely Large Telescope, aideront à trouver plus de lunes autour d’étoiles lointaines et à mieux voir ces systèmes étranges.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Pour la première fois, des astronomes ont trouvé de fortes preuves d’une énorme lune orbitant une naine brune hors de notre Système solaire, ce qui change notre compréhension des lunes et des planètes dans l’espace.
articles.personality_title_es: Astrónomos encuentran una posible luna gigante fuera de nuestro Sistema Solar
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han estado buscando lunas fuera de nuestro Sistema Solar durante muchos años. Aunque se han descubierto miles de planetas alrededor de otras estrellas, encontrar lunas que orbitan esos planetas ha sido mucho más difícil.

**Qué pasó** – Usando un telescopio muy potente en Chile, los astrónomos descubrieron un objeto muy grande que orbita una enana marrón, la cual a su vez orbita una estrella llamada CD-35 2722. Este objeto es al menos tan grande como Júpiter, mucho más grande que cualquier luna que conocemos. Como orbita una enana marrón (que está entre un planeta y una estrella), los científicos lo llaman un exosatélite. Es la primera vez que se detecta una posible luna así fuera de nuestro Sistema Solar.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento es inusual porque el objeto es enorme y no encaja claramente en las categorías de planeta o luna basadas en nuestro Sistema Solar. Esto desafía la manera en que los científicos definen lunas y planetas. Encontrar un exosatélite así nos ayuda a entender mejor cómo se organizan y forman los diferentes sistemas estelares.

**Próximo paso** – Los astrónomos seguirán estudiando el sistema CD-35 2722 para confirmar que el objeto es realmente una luna y no otra cosa. Nuevos telescopios, como el futuro Extremely Large Telescope, ayudarán a encontrar más lunas alrededor de estrellas lejanas y a obtener imágenes más claras de estos sistemas extraños.

**Frase clave** – Por primera vez, los astrónomos han encontrado pruebas fuertes de una luna gigante orbitando una enana marrón fuera de nuestro Sistema Solar, cambiando nuestra comprensión de lunas y planetas en el espacio.
